With a fluoroquinolone, review allergy, QT interval, interactions and fluoroquinolone risks. Immunocompromised patients need a separate assessment.

cards.t: Hospitalized community-acquired pneumonia: nonsevere and severe regimens
q: what antibiotics for nonsevere inpatient CAP
what is the regimen for severe CAP
when should you add MRSA or Pseudomonas coverage
cards.x:
Hospitalized community-acquired pneumonia is split into nonsevere and severe.
- Nonsevere, no methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA) or Pseudomonas risk: a beta-lactam (for example ceftriaxone or ampicillin/sulbactam) plus a macrolide, or a respiratory fluoroquinolone alone. Use a beta-lactam plus doxycycline when macrolides and fluoroquinolones are unsuitable.
- Severe (intensive care evaluation for vasopressor-dependent shock or respiratory failure needing ventilation): a beta-lactam plus azithromycin or a respiratory fluoroquinolone, with cultures and de-escalation. Review a severe beta-lactam allergy with pharmacy or infectious disease.

Extra coverage is added only for validated risks. For MRSA, use vancomycin or linezolid; for Pseudomonas, an active antipseudomonal agent (moxifloxacin and ertapenem are not reliable options). A prior respiratory MRSA isolate in severe pneumonia is a validated risk: add vancomycin or linezolid to the beta-lactam combination, obtain cultures and de-escalate as results return.

cards.t: How long to treat pneumonia and what to do if it worsens
q: how many days of antibiotics for pneumonia
do viral-positive patients still need antibiotics
what if pneumonia gets worse on treatment
cards.x:
How long to treat community-acquired pneumonia depends on severity and response. Nonsevere pneumonia that is clinically stable may use fewer than 5 days of antibiotics (minimum 3). Severe pneumonia needs at least 5 days and clinical stability.

A positive viral test can change the plan. Viral-positive outpatients without comorbidities may avoid empiric antibiotics with close follow-up. Viral-positive patients with comorbidities, and anyone hospitalized with community-acquired pneumonia, generally still need empiric antibacterial therapy.

If the patient worsens, reassess the diagnosis, adherence, resistance, abscess or empyema, or another complication.

cards.t: Hospital-acquired and ventilator-associated pneumonia treatment
q: how do you treat hospital-acquired pneumonia
what antibiotics for ventilator-associated pneumonia
how long is HAP or VAP treated
cards.x:
Hospital-acquired and ventilator-associated pneumonia are treated using the local antibiogram (the hospital's pattern of resistance), prior cultures and the patient's resistance risk, not the retired healthcare-associated category. Collect respiratory specimens first, then start empiric antibiotics without delaying care in unstable patients.
- No major resistance or high mortality risk: an antipseudomonal agent with methicillin-sensitive Staphylococcus aureus coverage, for example piperacillin/tazobactam or cefepime.
- Methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA) risk, resistance risk or high mortality risk: add vancomycin or linezolid when MRSA coverage is indicated, and a second antipseudomonal class for selected high-risk patients.

Reassess daily and de-escalate, narrowing or stopping as results clarify. The usual duration is 7 days if the response is adequate.

cards.t: Ventilator-associated pneumonia: why it happens and how to prevent it
q: why do ventilated patients get pneumonia
how do you prevent ventilator-associated pneumonia
why is VAP worse than other pneumonia
cards.x:
Ventilator-associated pneumonia (VAP) is pneumonia that starts more than 48 hours after a breathing tube is placed. The circuit is closed, but it still gets contaminated by flora, secretions, the hands of healthcare workers, circuit changes, biofilm on the tube and prior antibiotics. It carries higher mortality and longer intensive care unit stays, and Pseudomonas or multidrug-resistant organisms are more likely.

Prevention is the main thing:
- early extubation
- hand washing and sterile technique
- limiting circuit changes
- elevating the head of the bed
- supraglottic secretion drainage and mouth care

cards.t: Complications of community-acquired pneumonia
q: what are the complications of pneumonia
what is a parapneumonic effusion
what should you think of if pneumonia gets worse
cards.x:
Community-acquired pneumonia can lead to bacteremia and sepsis (infection spreading through the blood), respiratory failure, a parapneumonic effusion (fluid next to the pneumonia) and empyema, or a lung abscess. It can also be fatal; influenza and pneumonia together are the 8th leading cause of death.

These are the things to look for when a patient worsens: reassess the diagnosis, adherence, resistance, abscess or empyema, or another complication. A complicated parapneumonic effusion or empyema is drained when indicated.

cards.t: Aspiration pneumonitis versus aspiration pneumonia
q: what is the difference between aspiration pneumonitis and aspiration pneumonia
do you give antibiotics for aspiration pneumonitis
who is at risk for aspiration
cards.x:
Aspiration can cause two different problems, and they are treated differently.
- Aspiration pneumonitis is a sterile chemical injury, often after gastric contents enter the lungs. It typically shows abrupt respiratory decline after a witnessed aspiration, and fever or leukocytosis can occur without bacterial infection. Support oxygenation and the airway, and avoid prophylactic antibiotics when bacterial infection is not suspected. If it persists or worsens, think secondary infection, a complication or another diagnosis.
- Aspiration pneumonia is a bacterial infection after aspiration of colonized oropharyngeal material. It is an infectious syndrome with a compatible infiltrate and aspiration risk, and the event may be unwitnessed. Use the regimen for community- or hospital-acquired pneumonia by setting and severity; anaerobic coverage only for abscess or empyema, not routinely.

Risk factors are dysphagia, altered consciousness and impaired airway protection (stroke, seizure). Chemical injury needs support; established infection needs antibiotics.

cards.t: Lung abscess: causes, symptoms and imaging
q: what is a lung abscess
what are the signs of a lung abscess
what are amphoric breath sounds
cards.x:
A lung abscess is a cavitating infection of the lung that grows and damages tissue, often after aspiration. The pathogens listed are anaerobic oral flora, Mycobacterium tuberculosis, nontuberculous mycobacteria, and Staphylococcus aureus including methicillin-resistant strains.

It can be insidious and prolonged, lasting weeks and sometimes becoming chronic. Presentation includes fever, chills, sweats and cough, with purulent, foul-smelling sputum (aspiration is a likely cause), progressing to hemoptysis (coughing up blood) as the cavity grows. Pleuritic pain, dyspnea, malaise, tachycardia and tachypnea can occur. Findings include dullness, whispered pectoriloquy, bronchophony and amphoric breath sounds (low-pitched with high overtones, like breathing across an open jar). Film and computed tomography (CT) show a cavitary lesion with an air-fluid level.

cards.t: Lung abscess treatment
q: how is a lung abscess treated
why is clindamycin only an alternative for lung abscess
when does a lung abscess need drainage or surgery
cards.x:
Lung abscess treatment usually begins with antibiotics. The first choice is a beta-lactam/beta-lactamase inhibitor, such as intravenous ampicillin/sulbactam followed by oral amoxicillin/clavulanate. Clindamycin is reserved for selected alternatives because of the risk of Clostridioides difficile infection. Treatment commonly lasts several weeks, guided by clinical and radiographic response.

Computed tomography (CT) is part of the workup, and bronchoscopy is considered for obstruction, unusual pathogens or failure to improve. Large or refractory abscesses need pulmonary or infectious disease review for drainage or surgery. Routine chest physiotherapy is not essential.

cards.t: Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia (PJP)
q: what is Pneumocystis pneumonia
what does PJP look like in a patient
why is Pneumocystis called a fungal pneumonia if antibiotics treat it
cards.x:
Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia (PJP), formerly called Pneumocystis carinii pneumonia, is a lung infection that mostly hits people whose immune defenses are weak. It is the most common opportunistic infection (one that takes advantage of weak defenses) in people with human immunodeficiency virus (HIV). It is classified as a fungal pneumonia, yet antibiotics are the main treatment. Other risk factors are chemotherapy, anti-rejection drugs, long-term steroids, organ transplant and blood cancer.

The picture is progressive shortness of breath on exertion (about 95%), a nonproductive cough (about 95%) and fever (more than 80%), sometimes with chest discomfort, weight loss and chills. Coughing up blood is rare. The exam can show fast breathing, fever, a fast heart rate and mild crackles, but up to half of patients have a normal exam. The chest film shows diffuse bilateral infiltrates extending out from the perihilar region (around the center of each lung). Cases are falling with prophylaxis and antiretroviral therapy, but mortality is still 10-20%.

cards.t: How Pneumocystis pneumonia is diagnosed
q: how do you confirm Pneumocystis pneumonia
does a negative sputum rule out PJP
is beta-D-glucan specific for Pneumocystis
cards.x:
Pneumocystis pneumonia is confirmed by finding the organism in a lung sample: induced sputum or bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL, a fluid wash of the airways), examined under the microscope and/or tested with Pneumocystis polymerase chain reaction (PCR). PCR is highly sensitive but can detect colonization, meaning the organism is present without necessarily causing disease. A negative induced sputum does not exclude the infection: the next step is BAL. Sputum coughed up spontaneously has poor sensitivity.

The supporting tests are not specific. A low serum beta-D-glucan makes the infection less likely, especially with HIV, but it is not organism-specific, and a negative result alone cannot exclude it when suspicion is high. Lactate dehydrogenase is nonspecific and can neither confirm the infection nor show treatment failure. Offer HIV testing when status is unknown, and with HIV check the cluster of differentiation 4 (CD4) count and viral load. If suspicion is high, start treatment while the diagnosis is pursued.

cards.t: Pneumocystis pneumonia treatment and steroids
q: how is Pneumocystis pneumonia treated
when are steroids added for Pneumocystis
what do you check before primaquine or dapsone
cards.x:
Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole is the preferred treatment for Pneumocystis pneumonia. In HIV-associated disease it is given for 21 days and adjusted for kidney function. It goes in through a vein for moderate to severe disease, then by mouth once the patient improves. Alternatives depend on severity: clindamycin plus primaquine, intravenous pentamidine, or atovaquone for mild disease. Check glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD) before primaquine or dapsone, and monitor blood counts, creatinine, potassium and drug toxicity. Without HIV, the length of treatment is individualized with specialists.

Corticosteroids are added in HIV-associated disease when room-air arterial oxygen (PaO2) is below 70 mm Hg, or the alveolar-arterial gradient is 35 or more. They are started as early as possible, ideally within 72 hours of starting therapy. Evidence for steroids outside HIV is less certain. If a patient gets worse, reassess for toxicity, coinfection or treatment failure rather than switching drugs automatically.

cards.t: Preventing Pneumocystis pneumonia in HIV (prophylaxis)
k: when to start antiretroviral therapy with PJP
q: when do you give prophylaxis for Pneumocystis
what CD4 count needs Pneumocystis prophylaxis
when do you stop Pneumocystis prophylaxis
cards.x:
Prophylaxis means giving a drug to prevent an infection before it happens. In people with HIV, primary prophylaxis (before any episode of Pneumocystis pneumonia) is given when the cluster of differentiation 4 (CD4) count is below 100 cells/mm³, or 100-200 with detectable HIV RNA. Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole is the preferred drug. Secondary prophylaxis (to prevent a repeat episode) follows treatment of an infection, and prophylaxis is stopped only after immune recovery meets guideline-defined criteria.

Antiretroviral therapy is started within about 2 weeks of diagnosis when feasible. Patients should avoid sharing a room with other immunocompromised patients. Cases are falling with prophylaxis and antiretroviral therapy, but mortality is still 10-20%.

cards.t: Histoplasmosis (Histoplasma capsulatum)
k: bird or bat dropping lung infection
q: what is histoplasmosis
where do you get histoplasmosis
what are the symptoms of histoplasmosis
cards.x:
Histoplasmosis is a lung infection caused by the fungus Histoplasma capsulatum, which people breathe in from soil and from bird or bat droppings. Think of farming, gardening and cleaning chicken coops. In the United States it is found mainly in the central and eastern states, especially the Ohio and Mississippi River valleys, and it is rare.

Symptoms begin 3-17 days after inhaling the fungus: high fever, chills, myalgias (muscle aches), a nonproductive cough, chest pain and headache, so it can look like the flu. Some people have no symptoms at all, and the only sign is a granuloma (a small nodule) on the chest film. Possible complications are disseminated disease (spread beyond the lungs) and chronic cavitary disease.

cards.t: Histoplasmosis testing and treatment
q: how do you test for histoplasmosis
does a negative Histoplasma antigen rule it out
when is histoplasmosis treated with antifungals
cards.x:
The history is the first clue: ask about geography, soil disruption and bird or bat exposure. The main test is a urine Histoplasma antigen, often with serum antigen and antibody. Early negative tests do not exclude the infection, so repeat them or get respiratory specimens. The antigen can cross-react with Blastomyces (a different organism), meaning it may also react to that infection. Culture or histopathology is used for severe, persistent or uncertain cases.

Treatment depends on severity and the host:
- Mild acute disease in an adult with a normal immune system often needs observation, not antifungals.
- Itraconazole is used for prolonged or progressive illness or higher-risk hosts (monitor interactions and drug levels).
- Severe pulmonary or disseminated disease needs specialist-led amphotericin-based induction.
- Chronic cavitary disease needs azole therapy, usually for at least 12 months.

cards.t: Cryptococcosis (Cryptococcus neoformans and gattii)
q: what is cryptococcosis
how is cryptococcal lung disease diagnosed
how is cryptococcosis treated
cards.x:
Cryptococcosis is an infection with Cryptococcus neoformans or Cryptococcus gattii, caught by inhaling the organism from the environment. Risk rises with HIV, transplant or steroids, but disease also occurs in people who are not immunocompromised. In the lungs it causes cough and fever, with nodules or consolidation (a solid-looking patch of lung) on imaging, so it can mimic community-acquired pneumonia (CAP), tuberculosis or cancer. Headache or confusion suggests it has reached the central nervous system.

The workup is a serum cryptococcal antigen plus respiratory culture or histology, and an evaluation for central nervous system or disseminated disease, often with a lumbar puncture. Mild isolated pulmonary disease gets fluconazole, generally for 6-12 months. Severe pulmonary, central nervous system or disseminated disease gets induction with liposomal amphotericin B plus flucytosine, then fluconazole. Infectious disease consultation is part of the plan.

cards.t: Psittacosis (parrot fever)
q: what is psittacosis
how do people catch psittacosis
what symptoms point to psittacosis
cards.x:
Psittacosis, or parrot fever, is an atypical pneumonia caused by Chlamydia psittaci, an obligate intracellular bacterium (it can only live inside cells). It comes from parrots, parakeets, canaries and other birds, and it is rare, with about 200 patients a year. It is mainly an occupational disease: zoo and pet-shop workers, poultry farmers and ranchers. People catch it by inhaling the organism while handling sick birds, or through mouth-to-beak resuscitation. Spread from person to person is rare.

Symptoms are fever and cough (each in 50-90%, with the cough usually nonproductive), chills, malaise and shortness of breath. Sore throat, nosebleeds (epistaxis), and severe headache with photophobia (light sensitivity) are all common. Agitation and lethargy can occur, while pleuritic chest pain and gastrointestinal symptoms are rare. The quick clue is pneumonia plus severe headache and nosebleeds in someone who handles birds.

cards.t: Psittacosis exam findings, stages and chest film
q: what are Horder spots
what exam findings suggest psittacosis
what does psittacosis look like on a chest film
cards.x:
On exam the lung sounds are nonspecific. The helpful clues are relative bradycardia (a heart rate slower than the fever would lead you to expect), which is common, and splenomegaly (an enlarged spleen) in 10-70%. Horder spots are macular rashes (flat spots) that resemble the rose spots of typhoid fever, but they appear on the face. Hemolytic anemia is possible.

The illness moves through stages: a flu-like illness with a normal chest film, then mild to moderate pneumonia, then severe pneumonia, and finally respiratory failure and septic shock. The chest film is abnormal in up to 90%, most often with a dense unilateral infiltrate in a lower lobe. It can also be bilateral, nodular, miliary or interstitial, and it resolves in about 6 weeks (range 3-20).

cards.t: Psittacosis diagnosis and treatment
q: how do you diagnose psittacosis
how is psittacosis treated
why doesn't culture find psittacosis
cards.x:
Start with the history: ask about bird or poultry exposure. A respiratory nucleic acid amplification test (NAAT) or polymerase chain reaction (PCR) is timely and sensitive, and should be coordinated with public health laboratories. Serology needs paired samples and cross-reacts with other Chlamydia, and routine bacterial culture does not detect the organism. Blood counts and liver enzymes assess how sick the patient is, not the cause.

Doxycycline is the preferred treatment in adults, started promptly when psittacosis is strongly suspected. Improvement often comes within 48-72 hours, and treatment continues for 10-14 days after the fever resolves to prevent relapse. If tetracyclines are unsuitable, discuss a macrolide with infectious disease, since macrolide failures have occurred. Standard precautions are used: routine isolation and contact prophylaxis are not generally recommended. Report cases to public health per state rules, and arrange veterinary assessment of the birds and safe cleaning.

cards.t: Mycoplasma pneumoniae pneumonia (walking pneumonia)
q: what is Mycoplasma pneumonia
why don't beta-lactams work on Mycoplasma
how is Mycoplasma pneumonia treated
cards.x:
Mycoplasma pneumoniae causes an atypical pneumonia, sometimes called walking pneumonia because it can be milder. It is seen in school-age children and young adults, though adults get it too, and it spreads in household or group outbreaks. The onset is gradual: fever, a persistent cough and headache, with variable chest findings. Severe or extrapulmonary illness (outside the lungs) can occur, and the cough may persist. A respiratory nucleic acid amplification test is used when the result will change care.

Treatment in adults is a macrolide or doxycycline, with a respiratory fluoroquinolone as an alternative. Beta-lactams are ineffective because Mycoplasma has no cell wall. If a macrolide fails, reassess and consider doxycycline. Patients should return for shortness of breath or deterioration. There is no vaccine.

cards.t: Influenza virus: types, antigenic drift and antigenic shift
k: why the flu vaccine changes every year
q: what is the difference between antigenic drift and shift
why is the flu vaccine updated every year
which influenza type is most pathogenic
cards.x:
Influenza is a highly contagious airborne orthomyxovirus spread by droplet nuclei. It causes epidemics and pandemics, with the season starting in early fall, peaking in mid-February and ending in late spring. It also infects animals (birds, pigs, dogs, horses, seals) and can cross over to humans. There are types A, B and C. Influenza A is more pathogenic, causing most human infections and all avian infections, and its subtypes are named by hemagglutinin (H) and neuraminidase (N), two surface proteins.

The virus changes in two ways:
- Antigenic drift is a gradual series of point changes in the surface proteins. It produces new strains and loss of cross-protection, which is why vaccines are updated every year.
- Antigenic shift happens when the genes of two strains are reassorted during coinfection of one host. It produces novel strains and possibly more severe outbreaks.

cards.t: High-risk groups for severe influenza
k: who is high risk for influenza
q: who is at high risk for severe influenza
does travel make influenza high risk
should high-risk patients get antivirals after 48 hours
cards.x:
Some people are more likely to develop severe influenza. Risk status supports prompt antiviral treatment even after 48 hours of symptoms. Travel or animal exposure changes testing and public health needs, but it is not itself a risk factor for severe disease. The high-risk groups are:
- children under 5 (especially under 2) and adults 65 or older
- long-term care residents and people with immunocompromise
- people with chronic pulmonary, cardiac, renal, hepatic, hematologic, metabolic or neurologic disease
- pregnancy in any trimester and the first 2 weeks postpartum
- severe obesity

cards.t: Influenza symptoms and exam findings
q: what are the symptoms of influenza
what does the exam show in influenza
what else looks like influenza
cards.x:
Influenza hits suddenly, sometimes over as little as a day. Typical symptoms are cough, fever, sore throat (the reason most people seek care), myalgias (muscle aches), frontal or retro-orbital headache (behind the eyes), weakness and severe fatigue, and red watery eyes. Diarrhea occurs mostly in children. The incubation period is usually 1-4 days.

On exam the patient looks ill, with a fever of 100-104 °F, pharyngitis, red watery eyes, and wheezes or rhonchi in the lungs. The heart rate is fast from hypoxia or fever, and mild volume depletion shows up as dry skin. The differential includes adenovirus, enterovirus, paramyxovirus, cytomegalovirus and human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) infection.

cards.t: Testing for influenza
q: does a negative rapid flu test rule out influenza
which influenza test is preferred
should I wait for a test before treating influenza
cards.x:
Clinical suspicion can justify treatment: do not wait for confirmation in hospitalized, high-risk or progressively ill patients. When testing is needed, rapid molecular assays or reverse-transcription polymerase chain reaction (PCR) are preferred over rapid antigen tests, which have low sensitivity. Hospitalized patients get a molecular test, with a multiplex test for influenza and severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2) when both viruses are circulating.

A negative rapid antigen test does not exclude influenza. Confirm with molecular testing when it matters, and do not withhold antivirals while waiting. If a patient has severe lower-respiratory illness but a negative upper-airway test, consider a lower-respiratory specimen. Viral culture is used for surveillance. Being vaccinated does not exclude influenza in a symptomatic patient. A chest film is used to rule out pneumonia, especially in the elderly or high-risk.

cards.t: Influenza pneumonia (primary viral and secondary bacterial)
q: what is influenza pneumonia
which bacteria cause pneumonia after influenza
what does influenza pneumonia look like on a chest film
cards.x:
Influenza pneumonia is pneumonia during influenza, and it shows up as rapidly progressive cough, shortness of breath and cyanosis (a bluish color from low oxygen). It can be primary viral pneumonia, caused by the virus itself, or secondary bacterial pneumonia, which is often pneumococcal or staphylococcal. The chest film shows peribronchial and patchy interstitial infiltrates in several lobes with atelectasis (collapsed areas of lung), and possibly diffuse interstitial pneumonitis.

A chest film is advised to rule out pneumonia in influenza, especially in the elderly or high-risk. Antibiotics are used only if bacterial pneumonia is proven or suspected.

cards.t: Antiviral drugs for influenza
q: which antiviral is preferred for influenza
when is baloxavir not appropriate
why are amantadine and rimantadine not recommended
cards.x:
Which influenza antiviral fits depends on the patient:
- Oseltamivir is preferred for hospitalized, severe or progressive and high-risk patients, including in pregnancy. Start promptly even after 48 hours. The usual uncomplicated adult course is 5 days, adjusted for kidney function, and hospitalized patients generally receive oral or enteric oseltamivir.
- Baloxavir is a single-dose option for uncomplicated influenza within 48 hours in eligible patients aged 5 or older. It is not for pregnancy, breastfeeding, severe immunosuppression or hospitalized influenza, and coadministration with polyvalent cations should be avoided.
- Inhaled zanamivir is another option, but avoid it in asthma or chronic obstructive pulmonary disease because of bronchospasm.
- Intravenous peramivir is for eligible outpatients with uncomplicated influenza, adjusted for kidney function.
- Amantadine and rimantadine are not recommended because of resistance.

cards.t: Supportive care for influenza and when to return
q: why avoid aspirin in children with influenza
when should antibiotics be used with influenza
when should a patient with influenza come back
cards.x:
Most influenza care is supportive: rest and hydration. Fever often improves over several days, but cough and fatigue may persist. Patients should return urgently for shortness of breath, chest pain, dehydration, confusion, or improvement followed by worsening.

Antipyretics (fever reducers) such as acetaminophen and ibuprofen can be used, but avoid aspirin under 18 years because of Reye syndrome. Antibiotics are used only if bacterial pneumonia is proven or suspected.

cards.t: COVID-19: how it spreads and who is at risk
q: what causes COVID-19
how does COVID-19 spread
who is at high risk of severe COVID-19
cards.x:
Coronavirus disease (COVID-19) is caused by severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2). It spreads mainly when people inhale infectious respiratory particles, especially indoors with poor ventilation, and close contact increases exposure. Surface transmission is less important. Prevention rests on vaccination, ventilation, staying home when ill and risk-based masking.

Severity ranges from no symptoms to respiratory failure, and persistent symptoms can follow any severity. Age is a major predictor: risk rises substantially above 65. Immunocompromise, multiple chronic conditions and lack of current vaccination add risk. High-risk patients should contact a clinician early, because treatment windows are short.

cards.t: COVID-19 symptoms and incubation
q: what are the symptoms of COVID-19
how long is the COVID-19 incubation period
what else looks like COVID-19
cards.x:
After exposure, the median incubation is about 5 days, and symptoms usually appear within 11 days. Between 18% and 33% of infected people have no symptoms. The most common symptoms are cough, shortness of breath, fever, myalgia (muscle aches) and headache. Less common ones, depending on the strain, are sore throat, anosmia (loss of smell), dysgeusia (altered taste), anorexia, nausea or diarrhea.

Because the picture overlaps with other lung infections, the differential includes community-acquired pneumonia (CAP), other viral pneumonia, influenza, aspiration pneumonia, Pneumocystis pneumonia and pulmonary tuberculosis. Severe disease shows marked tachypnea (fast breathing) and an oxygen saturation below 94% on room air.

cards.t: Testing for COVID-19
q: what is the most sensitive test for COVID-19
what if a COVID antigen test is negative
does a high D-dimer diagnose a clot in COVID-19
cards.x:
A nucleic acid amplification test (NAAT), including polymerase chain reaction (PCR), is the most sensitive routine test for coronavirus disease (COVID-19). One negative antigen test does not exclude infection. Repeat it after 48 hours (at least 2 tests if the person has symptoms, 3 if not) or get a NAAT.

Imaging evaluates pneumonia and complications, not the virus itself. Hospital tests should each answer a clinical question: organ function, oxygenation, coinfection or thrombosis (blood clots). An elevated D-dimer alone does not diagnose thrombosis or set the intensity of anticoagulation.

cards.t: COVID-19 severity categories
q: how is COVID-19 severity classified
what makes COVID-19 severe instead of moderate
what decides the COVID-19 treatment pathway
cards.x:
Severity is stratified first, and oxygenation and severity, not a positive test or elapsed time alone, decide the treatment pathway. The five categories are:
- Asymptomatic or presymptomatic: infection without symptoms.
- Mild: some symptoms, no shortness of breath, a normal chest film.
- Moderate: some symptoms, a positive chest film and oxygen saturation of at least 94% on room air.
- Severe: saturation below 94% on room air, marked tachypnea, infiltrates over 50% of lung volume.
- Critical: acute respiratory failure, septic shock or multiple organ dysfunction.

cards.t: COVID-19 treatment for high-risk outpatients
q: how is COVID-19 treated in a high-risk outpatient
when is molnupiravir used
should steroids be given for COVID-19 without hypoxemia
cards.x:
For high-risk outpatients with mild or moderate coronavirus disease (COVID-19) and no hypoxemia (low blood oxygen), the options are nirmatrelvir/ritonavir within 5 days, or a 3-day course of intravenous remdesivir within 7 days of symptom onset. Before nirmatrelvir/ritonavir, review drug interactions, kidney dosing and liver contraindications; it is approved for adults. Molnupiravir is an adult alternative only when the preferred options are unsuitable, and it should be avoided in pregnancy.

Systemic steroids are not given for COVID-19 without hypoxemia unless there is another indication. Treatment windows are short, which is why high-risk patients should contact a clinician early.

cards.t: COVID-19 treatment for hospitalized patients with hypoxemia
q: how is hospitalized COVID-19 with low oxygen treated
what steroid is used for hypoxemic COVID-19
should D-dimer decide full-dose anticoagulation
cards.x:
For hospitalized adults with hypoxemia, dexamethasone, a corticosteroid, is given for up to 10 days or until discharge. Consider remdesivir, judged by timing and the level of respiratory support. If the illness progresses rapidly, baricitinib or tocilizumab plus corticosteroids may be warranted. Oxygen or ventilatory support is given as needed.

Venous thromboembolism prophylaxis (blood-clot prevention) is given unless contraindicated. Therapeutic-intensity anticoagulation needs a thrombosis and bleeding assessment, not a D-dimer alone.

cards.t: Pneumonia in older adults
q: how does age affect pneumonia severity scores
why are older adults prone to aspiration pneumonia
what should I watch for with influenza or COVID-19 in older adults
cards.x:
Pneumonia has its highest incidence over 65, and two scoring tools, the Pneumonia Severity Index (PSI) and a score built from confusion, urea, respiratory rate, blood pressure and age 65 (CURB-65), drive the treatment setting. Age 65 or older is one point on CURB-65, while the PSI adds a point per year of age and adds 10 for nursing-home residence.

Aspiration is a risk with seizure or altered consciousness and, in older adults, with dysphagia (trouble swallowing): assess swallowing, oral hygiene and positioning. People 65 and older and long-term care residents are high-risk for influenza, so treat early and get a chest film to rule out pneumonia. Risk from coronavirus disease (COVID-19) also rises substantially above 65.

cards.t: Which tests to order for suspected pneumonia
k: when to get a CT in pneumonia
q: what tests do you order for pneumonia
when is a CT needed for pneumonia
do all outpatients with pneumonia need cultures
cards.x:
Order a test only to answer a specific management question: routine cultures, blood counts or computed tomography (CT) do not help every stable outpatient. Four questions guide the workup:
- Is pneumonia present? A chest radiograph, or lung ultrasound with expertise, confirms a lung-tissue process and separates pneumonia from bronchitis or another diagnosis.
- Where to treat? Saturation, vital signs, organ dysfunction, a sepsis assessment and the Pneumonia Severity Index (PSI) plus judgment decide outpatient, ward or intensive care.
- Will the result change initial therapy or precautions? Molecular viral testing, and cultures for severe pneumonia or validated resistance risk, guide antivirals, infection prevention, targeted coverage and later de-escalation.
- Is the course atypical or complicated? CT for uncertainty, cavitation, obstruction, abscess or empyema, and targeted tests by exposure or immune status, find a complication or another cause.

cards.t: When antibiotics should be withheld
q: when should antibiotics be withheld
do you give antibiotics for acute bronchitis
do you give antibiotics for influenza or COVID-19
cards.x:
Antibiotics treat a bacterial syndrome, not cough duration, sputum color, a positive viral test or inflammation alone. When they are withheld, set a safety net: expected-course counseling, explicit return precautions and a plan for reassessment. Antibiotics can be withheld in these situations:
- uncomplicated acute bronchitis, whatever the sputum color or duration
- chemical aspiration pneumonitis, which gets supportive care and no prophylactic antibiotics
- influenza or coronavirus disease (COVID-19) without a bacterial complication, which follows the antiviral and supportive pathway
- a selected viral-positive outpatient with community-acquired pneumonia, no comorbidities and reliable close follow-up

cards.t: When antibiotics are needed or the course needs rethinking
q: when should antibiotics be started for pneumonia
how do you treat aspiration pneumonia with abscess or empyema
what do you do if pneumonia is getting worse
cards.x:
Treat the bacterial infection that is actually there, and rethink when the course goes wrong:
- Suspected bacterial pneumonia: treat promptly on the community-acquired or hospital-acquired pneumonia pathway.
- Severe or unstable patient: obtain specimens without delaying empiric (best-guess) therapy.
- Aspiration pneumonia, abscess or empyema: treat the infection, with anaerobic coverage for abscess or empyema.
- A worsening course: reassess the diagnosis, resistance, adherence and complications rather than adding drugs.

cards.t: Mycobacteria and the acid-fast smear
q: what are acid-fast bacilli
can an acid-fast smear tell tuberculosis from nontuberculous mycobacteria
why does tuberculosis take so long to culture
cards.x:
Mycobacteria are acid-fast bacilli: rod-shaped bacteria with lipid-rich cell walls that contain mycolic acids. Mycobacterium tuberculosis grows slowly, so a culture can take weeks to come back, while molecular tests give rapid results.

The trap is the acid-fast smear. It identifies a group of organisms, not a single one, so a positive smear does not distinguish tuberculosis from nontuberculous mycobacteria (NTM), the many environmental species that include both slow and rapid growers. Think of the smear as saying "an acid-fast organism is here," not "this is tuberculosis."

cards.t: Mycobacterium tuberculosis complex versus nontuberculous mycobacteria
q: what species cause tuberculosis
what are the nontuberculous mycobacteria
why does it matter which mycobacterium it is
why do we only test some people for tuberculosis
cards.x:
Mycobacteria split into two groups that matter clinically. The Mycobacterium tuberculosis complex causes tuberculosis: M. tuberculosis is the principal human pathogen, and M. bovis and M. africanum belong to the complex too. Nontuberculous mycobacteria (NTM) include Mycobacterium avium complex (MAC), M. kansasii and M. abscessus. Knowing the species matters because transmission and treatment differ.

On the bigger picture, tuberculosis is the leading cause of death from a single infectious agent worldwide, and about a quarter of the world has been infected, yet it is preventable and curable. In the United States most cases occur in people born outside the country and most residents are low risk, so testing is aimed at people with exposure risk or a higher risk of progressing to disease rather than at everyone.

cards.t: Tuberculosis stages: infection versus disease
q: what is the difference between latent tuberculosis and active tuberculosis
what is reactivation tuberculosis
can someone with latent tuberculosis spread it
what is progressive primary tuberculosis
cards.x:
The key question is whether a person is merely infected or actually has disease, because that decides infectiousness, evaluation and treatment. There are four stages to keep straight:
- Primary infection: the first infection with Mycobacterium tuberculosis, which may stay contained without causing clinical disease.
- Progressive primary tuberculosis: disease develops soon after the first infection because the immune system fails to contain it.
- Latent tuberculosis infection: infected but with no symptoms, and no evidence of disease after clinical evaluation. The chest film is usually normal. The person is not infectious and cannot spread the disease.
- Reactivation (secondary) tuberculosis: a latent infection progresses to disease, often when immunity is impaired. Reinfection is a separate event from reactivation.

cards.t: Tuberculosis as a granulomatous disease and miliary spread
q: what is miliary tuberculosis
why can tuberculosis reactivate years later
how does tuberculosis spread to other organs
cards.x:
Tuberculosis is a chronic granulomatous disease, usually of the lung, but it can reach any organ by hematogenous spread, meaning it travels through the blood.

The first exposure usually triggers an immune reaction that quells the infection and gives resistance. But foci of infection can still harbor living organisms for years, and they can reactivate when immunity falls. In someone who is immunocompromised, primary or reactivated disease can become massive: a life-threatening systemic infection called miliary tuberculosis, with healed lesions, latent lesions, caseation, cavities and massive spread through the blood to organs such as the liver and spleen.

cards.t: How tuberculosis spreads and who is infectious
q: how is tuberculosis transmitted
is extrapulmonary tuberculosis contagious
what raises the risk of catching tuberculosis
cards.x:
Tuberculosis spreads through the air. Pulmonary and laryngeal tuberculosis release infectious aerosols when the person coughs, speaks or sings, and the risk rises with prolonged time sharing indoor air with poor ventilation.

Who does not spread it matters just as much. Latent infection does not transmit. Extrapulmonary disease (outside the lungs) usually is not infectious either, unless there is also pulmonary or laryngeal involvement or an aerosol-generating source.

Exposure risk comes from close contact with infectious tuberculosis, prolonged time in enclosed, poorly ventilated spaces, living or working where transmission is ongoing, or travel to or residence in high-incidence areas.

cards.t: Risk factors for progressing from tuberculosis infection to disease
q: who is at higher risk of developing active tuberculosis
why test someone before a tumor necrosis factor inhibitor
what medical conditions raise tuberculosis risk
cards.x:
Exposure decides who gets infected; a different set of factors decides who goes on to develop disease. The ones that raise the risk of progression are:
- HIV (human immunodeficiency virus) or major immunosuppression
- tumor necrosis factor (TNF) inhibitors, transplantation or prolonged corticosteroids
- recent infection, especially within 2 years
- infancy and young childhood
- diabetes mellitus
- chronic kidney disease or dialysis
- silicosis, low body weight or malnutrition
- tobacco use and harmful alcohol use

This is why a patient about to start a TNF inhibitor is tested for tuberculosis infection: testing is targeted at people at increased risk, and that medication puts them in the higher-progression-risk group.

cards.t: Pulmonary tuberculosis: presentation and differential
q: what are the symptoms of pulmonary tuberculosis
does a normal physical examination rule out tuberculosis
what else looks like tuberculosis
should I wait 3 weeks of cough before evaluating
cards.x:
Pulmonary tuberculosis (tuberculosis in the lungs) presents with a persistent cough with or without sputum, fever and night sweats, plus weight loss, reduced appetite and fatigue. Coughing up blood (hemoptysis) or chest pain that worsens with breathing (pleuritic pain) may occur, but dramatic hemoptysis is not required for the diagnosis. Symptoms can be mild or even absent, so do not wait 3 weeks to evaluate a high-risk patient.

The physical examination has limited sensitivity: crackles, bronchial breath sounds, fever, wasting or swollen lymph nodes (lymphadenopathy) are clues, but a normal examination does not exclude it. Children, older adults and immunocompromised patients may present atypically.

The differential is broad: nontuberculous mycobacterial (NTM) pulmonary disease, bacterial pneumonia or lung abscess, endemic fungal infection such as histoplasmosis, bronchiectasis or chronic pulmonary aspergillosis, and lung cancer and other causes of cavitary disease.

cards.t: Extrapulmonary tuberculosis
q: what organs can tuberculosis affect besides the lungs
how does tuberculosis present in the spine or brain
what does extrapulmonary tuberculosis look like
cards.x:
Extrapulmonary tuberculosis is disease outside the lungs, and it can involve almost any organ. How it looks depends on where it lands:
- Lymph nodes: persistent, often painless enlargement.
- Pleura: effusion, pleuritic pain and shortness of breath (dyspnea).
- Central nervous system: headache, meningismus (a stiff neck) and altered mental status.
- Spine: back pain, vertebral destruction and neurologic deficits.
- Disseminated disease: fever, weight loss and involvement of several organs.

Because the organ matters, organ-specific specimens and urgent assessment may be needed.

cards.t: Testing for tuberculosis infection: the skin test and the blood test
k: how to read a skin test
q: what is the Mantoux test and how is it read
does a positive skin test mean active tuberculosis
when do you measure a skin test
do you measure the redness
cards.x:
The tuberculin skin test (TST) and the interferon-gamma release assay (IGRA, a blood test) both detect the immune system's response to infection. Neither can tell latent infection from disease. A positive result needs clinical evaluation and chest imaging, and symptoms or suspicious imaging need microbiologic testing even when the TST or IGRA is negative. Testing is targeted at people at increased risk.

For the Mantoux skin test, purified protein derivative (PPD) is injected intradermally (into the skin) on the forearm. A trained reader checks it at 48 to 72 hours and measures the transverse induration, the firm raised area, in millimeters. Do not measure the redness (erythema). The result is then interpreted by the patient's risk category.

cards.t: Skin test positivity thresholds: 5, 10 and 15 mm
q: when is a skin test positive
what size induration is positive for a transplant recipient
what cutoff applies to a recent immigrant from a high-incidence area
what is the cutoff for a low-risk person
cards.x:
How big the induration (the firm raised area) must be, in millimeters (mm), to count as positive depends on the person's risk:
- 5 mm or more: HIV (human immunodeficiency virus), recent close contact, transplant, major immunosuppression, or imaging suggesting prior tuberculosis.
- 10 mm or more: increased exposure risk, selected medical risks, high-risk congregate settings, children under 5, or those exposed to high-risk adults.
- 15 mm or more: no known tuberculosis risk factors.

When a patient fits more than one line, use the most specific one. A transplant recipient is read at 5 mm because transplant is named in that line, even though "selected medical risks" sits in the 10 mm line. Travel to or residence in a high-incidence area is an exposure risk, so a recent arrival from such an area is read at 10 mm. A child under 5 with no known contact is also read at 10 mm.

cards.t: BCG vaccination and tuberculosis tests
q: does BCG cause a false positive skin test
which test is better for someone who had BCG
does BCG cause a positive IGRA
cards.x:
BCG (bacille Calmette-Guérin) vaccination and exposure to some nontuberculous mycobacteria can cause a false-positive tuberculin skin test (TST). Even so, the skin test is still read with the standard risk-based thresholds regardless of BCG history. For most patients who have had BCG, the blood test, the interferon-gamma release assay (IGRA), is preferred, and BCG vaccination does not cause a positive IGRA.

A positive result in either test still needs evaluation for disease before any preventive treatment is started.

cards.t: The IGRA blood test and what its results mean
q: what does a positive IGRA mean
what do you do with an indeterminate IGRA
should I repeat the skin test or IGRA to monitor treatment
does a negative IGRA rule out tuberculosis
cards.x:
The interferon-gamma release assay (IGRA) is a blood test, and two blood tests approved by the US Food and Drug Administration measure the immune response to tuberculosis-specific antigens. It needs only one visit for the specimen.

How to read it:
- Positive: means infection and requires evaluation for disease.
- Negative: infection is less likely, but disease remains possible.
- Indeterminate, invalid or borderline: repeat the IGRA or use a skin test.

Recent exposure and immunosuppression reduce its sensitivity. And since the skin test and the IGRA may stay positive after treatment, therapy is monitored by clinical and microbiologic response, not by repeating either test.

cards.t: Negative skin test or IGRA after recent exposure
q: when do you repeat a tuberculosis test after exposure
can a negative skin test be wrong
what if a symptomatic patient has a negative IGRA
cards.x:
A negative test does not always mean the person is clear. Early infection can still give a negative tuberculin skin test (TST) or interferon-gamma release assay (IGRA), so when indicated the test is repeated 8 to 10 weeks after the last exposure. Immunosuppression or severe tuberculosis may also cause false negatives.

If the patient has symptoms or there is high suspicion, evaluate for disease now rather than relying on the negative result. Young children and immunocompromised contacts need prompt public-health assessment.

cards.t: Testing sputum for pulmonary tuberculosis
q: how many sputum samples for tuberculosis
what tests are done on sputum for tuberculosis
what is the workup for suspected pulmonary tuberculosis
cards.x:
Testing for disease, as opposed to infection, combines sputum testing with chest imaging. For suspected pulmonary tuberculosis, the sputum work-up is:
- Collect 3 sputum specimens, 8 to 24 hours apart, with at least one early-morning specimen.
- Request an acid-fast bacilli (AFB) smear and a mycobacterial culture.
- Perform a rapid molecular test on at least one respiratory specimen.
- Obtain molecular and culture-based drug-susceptibility testing.
- Offer HIV (human immunodeficiency virus) testing when the status is unknown.

Drug-susceptibility testing checks which drugs the organism responds to, and it is done both by molecular methods and by culture.

cards.t: Chest imaging in tuberculosis
q: what does tuberculosis look like on chest x-ray
can imaging confirm tuberculosis
where does reactivation tuberculosis show up in the lungs
what does a latent tuberculosis chest film look like
cards.x:
Chest radiography is part of the initial evaluation, and computed tomography (CT) clarifies findings or complications. Findings include infiltrates, cavities, nodules, adenopathy and effusion; miliary disease can produce diffuse tiny nodules. Imaging supports suspicion but cannot confirm tuberculosis or reliably show whether it is active, and films cannot tell recent infection, reactivation or reinfection apart.

The pattern depends on the type. Primary disease may show hilar or mediastinal adenopathy (enlarged lymph nodes), infiltrates or effusion. Post-primary (reactivation) disease often involves the upper lobes and may cavitate. HIV (human immunodeficiency virus) and other immunosuppression give atypical patterns. Latent infection usually has a normal film.

Scarring, volume loss or calcified granulomas may reflect prior infection. Fibrotic lesions warrant review of prior treatment and exclusion of active disease, persistent shortness of breath after tuberculosis may reflect bronchiectasis or other lung injury, and new symptoms need reassessment for recurrence and alternatives.

cards.t: Isolation and reporting for presumed pulmonary tuberculosis
q: what precautions for suspected pulmonary tuberculosis
who do you report tuberculosis to
when can isolation end
what respirator should staff wear
cards.x:
When pulmonary tuberculosis is presumed or confirmed, do three things right away:
- Notify the local or state tuberculosis program.
- Use an airborne infection isolation room when indicated. Staff wear a fit-tested respirator, and the patient uses source control during transport, meaning steps that keep infectious aerosols from spreading.
- End isolation by clinical, laboratory and public-health criteria, not a fixed treatment interval. The number of days on treatment alone does not decide it.

cards.t: Standard treatment of drug-susceptible pulmonary tuberculosis
q: what is the standard tuberculosis regimen
when can ethambutol be stopped
how do you monitor tuberculosis treatment
what if the tuberculosis is rifampin resistant
cards.x:
Standard treatment for drug-susceptible pulmonary tuberculosis lasts 6 months: 2 months of isoniazid, rifampin, pyrazinamide and ethambutol, then 4 months of isoniazid and rifampin. Ethambutol can stop once susceptibility to isoniazid and rifampin is established. Daily therapy with directly observed therapy (DOT) or video DOT, where treatment is watched, supports completion. Some patients need longer or alternative regimens.

Monitoring: review adherence, symptoms and adverse effects at least monthly, follow sputum cultures until conversion and document the response at 2 months, and watch for liver injury, drug interactions and drug-specific toxicity. Rifampin resistance requires rapid susceptibility testing and expert management.

cards.t: Shorter treatment regimens for pulmonary tuberculosis
q: who can get the 17 week tuberculosis regimen
what is the shorter regimen for children with tuberculosis
what is in the rifapentine-moxifloxacin regimen
cards.x:
Two shorter options exist for susceptible disease:
- Age 12 or older: a 17-week rifapentine-moxifloxacin regimen, which is 8 weeks of isoniazid, rifapentine, pyrazinamide and moxifloxacin, then 9 weeks of isoniazid, rifapentine and moxifloxacin.
- Selected children with nonsevere disease: 4 months, which is 2 months of isoniazid, rifampin and pyrazinamide (with or without ethambutol), then 2 months of isoniazid and rifampin.

Eligibility, interactions and the site of disease need expert review.

cards.t: Treating latent tuberculosis infection
q: how is latent tuberculosis treated
what is 3HP
when do you use isoniazid for 6 or 9 months
what must you do before treating latent tuberculosis
cards.x:
Latent tuberculosis infection is treated only after tuberculosis disease has been excluded. The preferred short regimens are:
- Weekly isoniazid plus rifapentine for 3 months (3HP).
- Daily rifampin for 4 months (4R).
- Daily isoniazid plus rifampin for 3 months (3HR).

A longer alternative, isoniazid alone for 6 or 9 months (6H or 9H), is used when rifamycin regimens are unsuitable. Whichever regimen is chosen, check for drug interactions, pregnancy considerations and resistance in the source case.

cards.t: Nontuberculous mycobacterial lung disease and how it is diagnosed
q: how do you diagnose nontuberculous mycobacterial lung disease
does a positive sputum culture prove NTM disease
who gets Mycobacterium avium complex lung disease
is NTM contagious
cards.x:
Nontuberculous mycobacterial lung disease is caused by environmental mycobacteria. Mycobacterium avium complex (MAC) is a common cause, and M. kansasii and M. abscessus are among the others. Most infections come from the environment and person-to-person spread is uncommon. Risk rises with bronchiectasis, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) and immune dysfunction. Patients have a chronic cough and sputum, fatigue, weight loss or reduced appetite, and shortness of breath (dyspnea) or coughing up blood (hemoptysis); computed tomography (CT) may show nodular bronchiectasis or fibrocavitary disease.

A respiratory isolate alone does not prove disease. Diagnosis needs all three domains:
- Clinical and imaging: compatible symptoms and imaging.
- Exclusion: alternative diagnoses excluded.
- Microbiologic: usually 2 or more sputum cultures with the same species, or one positive bronchial wash or lavage or a qualifying biopsy.

cards.t: Treating Mycobacterium avium complex lung disease
q: how long is Mycobacterium avium complex treated
what drugs treat MAC lung disease
when is inhaled amikacin added
cards.x:
Macrolide-susceptible Mycobacterium avium complex lung disease is treated, under specialist direction, with azithromycin, ethambutol and a rifamycin. Treatment continues for at least 12 months after culture conversion. The clock starts at conversion, when cultures turn negative, not at the first dose.

Cavitary or severe disease may need daily therapy and initial intravenous amikacin, and cultures that are still positive after 6 months or more may warrant inhaled liposomal amikacin. Other nontuberculous mycobacterial species need different, susceptibility-guided regimens.

cards.t: Referral, public health and prognosis in tuberculosis
q: when do you notify public health about tuberculosis
what needs specialist direction in tuberculosis
is tuberculosis curable
how does tuberculosis differ in older adults
cards.x:
Notify the local or state tuberculosis program about any presumed or confirmed disease. Young children and immunocompromised contacts need prompt public-health assessment. Rifampin resistance, shorter regimens and treatment of nontuberculous mycobacterial disease need expert or specialist direction.

In adults and older adults the same targeting and thresholds apply: testing is aimed at exposure risk and progression risk, skin test thresholds of 5, 10 and 15 mm are used regardless of age or BCG (bacille Calmette-Guérin) vaccine history, and immunosuppression can cause false negatives, so symptomatic patients are evaluated for disease right away. Presentation may be atypical, and a normal examination does not exclude disease.

The outlook is good: tuberculosis is preventable and curable, and timely diagnosis, completion of treatment and preventive therapy protect both patients and communities.
